title: Forklift Safety on Construction Sites
summary: Forklifts cause many injuries and deaths each year through tip-overs, falling loads, and struck-by incidents. This talk covers training, daily inspection, travel, and load handling.
talking_points: Only trained and certified workers operate a forklift.
Inspect the forklift every day before use. Report any damage or problems during the shift to your supervisor.
Wear the seat belt if the forklift has one. On a stand-up, rear-entry forklift, exit by stepping backward if it starts to tip sideways.
Use extreme caution on grades and ramps. Tilt the load back and raise it only enough to clear the surface.
Do not raise or lower the forks while the forklift is moving.
Travel with a clear view of the path - drive in reverse if the load blocks your view. Sound the horn at corners and blind spots. Band or secure loads that could fall.
site_hazards_to_check: Untrained or uncertified workers operating the forklift
Skipped daily inspection, or known defects not tagged out
Steep grades, ramps, soft ground, or floor openings on the travel route
Loads that are loose, unbanded, or too tall to see over
Pedestrians in the forklift travel path or at blind corners
discussion_questions: What do you check during the daily forklift inspection?
What do you do when the load blocks your forward view?
How do we keep foot traffic separated from the forklift today?

flags: OSHA mapping verified accurate: 29 CFR 1926.602 (material handling equipment - 602(c) covers powered industrial trucks and references 1910.178) and 1910.178 (powered industrial trucks). Operator training/certification (1910.178(l)), daily pre-use inspection (1910.178(q)(7)), seat belt use, caution on grades, load tilted back and low, no raising/lowering forks while moving, drive in reverse when the load blocks the view, horn at blind corners - all consistent with the standard.
